Listen to a talk in an art history class.

Let's compare three movements from around the turn of the twentieth century. First, the Impressionists. They wanted to capture the changing effects of light, so they often painted outdoors, quickly, with loose brushstrokes. Claude Monet, for example, painted the same haystacks again and again at different times of day, just to show how the light changed. Then came the Expressionists. They weren't interested in what things looked like; they wanted to show emotion. So they distorted shapes and used intense, unnatural colors. Think of Edvard Munch's The Scream. And finally, Cubism. Painters like Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque broke objects into geometric shapes and showed them from several viewpoints at the same time, so you might see the front and the side of a face at once. Light, emotion, and multiple viewpoints. Those are the three ideas to keep apart.
Listen to a talk in a geology class.

Geologists sort rocks into three groups based on how they form. Igneous rocks form when melted rock, called magma, cools and hardens. Granite is a common example. The size of the crystals tells you how fast the magma cooled: slow cooling deep underground gives large crystals, while fast cooling at the surface gives tiny ones. Sedimentary rocks form differently. Small particles, like sand or mud, settle in layers, and over time those layers are pressed together. Sandstone is one example. Because the layers build up slowly, sedimentary rocks are where we usually find fossils. Finally, metamorphic rocks are existing rocks that have been changed by intense heat and pressure, without melting. Marble, for instance, forms when limestone is changed in this way.
Listen to a talk in a business class.

When a company launches a new product, how should it set the price? Let's look at three strategies. With penetration pricing, a company starts with a low price. The goal is to attract a lot of customers quickly and win market share. Later, once people are loyal, the price can go up. Price skimming is the opposite. The company starts with a high price, aimed at early adopters who are willing to pay more to have the product first, and then lowers the price over time. New smartphones are a good example. They're most expensive in the first few months. Finally, value-based pricing ignores production costs and competitors' prices. Instead, the price is based on how much customers believe the product is worth to them. So: start low, start high, or price by perceived value.

Listen to a talk in an Earth science class.

You may have heard the word supervolcano in the news. The term refers to a volcano capable of an eruption that throws out more than one thousand cubic kilometers of material. That's thousands of times larger than a typical eruption. Now, when people imagine the danger, they usually picture rivers of lava. But lava moves slowly and only affects the area near the volcano. The primary danger from a supereruption is actually ash. Ash can spread across an entire continent, collapse roofs, ruin crops, and block sunlight long enough to cool the global climate for several years.
Listen to a talk in a history class.

Construction of the Erie Canal began in 1817, and many people thought the project was foolish. But when the canal opened in 1825, it connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean through New York. Shipping costs between the Midwest and New York City fell by about ninety percent, and New York became the country's leading port. The canal's success didn't last forever, though. By the 1850s, railroads could move goods faster and all year round, while the canal froze in winter. So traffic on the canal gradually declined.
